Summary incorporating SLOOS lens:
- Policy stance and operations: The FOMC held the target range at 4.25–4.50%, kept IORB at 4.4%, ON RRP at 4.25%, and ON repo at 4.5%, maintaining a restrictive floor-system stance. It will slow Treasury runoff by cutting the monthly redemption cap from $25B to $5B starting in April, while keeping the MBS cap at $35B—an incremental dovish tilt to QT aimed at supporting market functioning. One dissent favored maintaining the faster runoff.
- Financial stability context: Ongoing vulnerabilities—particularly CRE stress, bank interest-rate risk tied to fixed-rate/HTM portfolios and uninsured deposits, large MMF footprint and leverage in market structure, tighter credit conditions, and elevated macro/geopolitical risks—reinforce a cautious posture. Slower Treasury runoff modestly reduces liquidity strain without materially easing policy.
- SLOOS read-through:
  • Demand: Banks report stronger demand across credit categories—C&I (including large, middle-market, and small firms), CRE, residential real estate, credit cards, and autos—signaling resilient underlying activity.  
  • Supply/underwriting: Standards remain tight, with many banks raising minimum credit score requirements for consumer loans and citing the economic outlook, industry-specific problems, and lower risk tolerance as key reasons.  
  • Credit quality: Banks expect higher delinquencies and charge-offs ahead, pointing to late-cycle credit normalization and a constraint on credit availability even if rates are unchanged.
Interpretation: Solid growth and low, stable unemployment support the rate hold, while SLOOS indicates that the bank-lending channel remains restrictive and credit risks are building. This combination argues for risk management and validates the decision to slow QT to ease potential market-functioning frictions. Net tone: balanced-to-cautious—macro resilience tempered by tighter underwriting and worsening credit expectations.
